record_sources.title: record-01-record
record_sources.quote: "Q. And how long did you live at the Bakers residence? A. Four to -- a little over four years" and "A. ... There was no handrail. I went completely down the steps...."

challenges.judge_assessment: This exposes a real overstatement in the brief. R.C. 5321.04(A)(2)'s habitability duty is not the statute's only potentially relevant duty; subsection (A)(1) separately requires compliance with applicable safety codes, and a qualifying violation can support negligence per se. Thus, proving that a missing handrail does not alone make premises uninhabitable does not establish that Ohio law never requires a handrail. Still, Friese cannot defeat summary judgment merely by saying a code may exist. On this record, no particular applicable code or violation is identified, and the brief contends no statutory claim was pleaded. Baker risks losing her categorical 'no statutory duty' proposition, but not necessarily the motion itself.
challenges.suggested_response: Friese cannot rely on R.C. 5321.04(A)(2) to transform the absence of a handrail into a habitability claim. Ohio authority holds that the common-law warranty of habitability does not, standing alone, make a premises substantially or wholly uninhabitable merely because a stairway lacks a handrail. Friese has not identified any applicable building, housing, health, or safety code under R.C. 5321.04(A)(1), and the record before the Court contains no evidence of a code violation. On this record, Baker is entitled to judgment on the statutory theory actually supported by the pleadings and evidence.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Qualify the handrail section so it does not say Ohio law never requires a handrail. Say only that the missing handrail does not itself make the premises uninhabitable under R.C. 5321.04(A)(2), and that Friese has not identified any applicable code under R.C. 5321.04(A)(1) or evidence of a violation.

A reasonable jury could find that the condition was not open and obvious due to poor lighting.

challenges.judge_assessment: A genuine lighting dispute could prevent a finding that the stair condition was objectively open and obvious, but the attack does not presently establish that dispute because the contrary deposition passage is not reproduced. More importantly, the pleaded hazard is the absence of a handrail, which Friese admittedly knew about and had reported to Baker. Poor lighting would not conceal the known absence of a railing. The attack becomes more consequential only if Friese identifies a different hazard—such as an obscured step configuration—as the cause of the fall. That is difficult on the quoted testimony, where he did not know why he missed the step. Baker risks losing the objective open-and-obvious characterization, but her actual-knowledge argument remains.
challenges.suggested_response: Even if Friese contends the lighting was less than ideal, that does not create a genuine issue of material fact on the open-and-obvious defense to the claim pleaded here. The hazard identified in the Complaint is the absence of a handrail, and Friese admitted he knew the stairs lacked a railing before January 16, 2021. He also testified that he used the stairs three to four times each day for nearly four years and could not say for certain why he missed the step. A dispute about lighting therefore does not defeat summary judgment on the known condition Friese claims caused his fall. At most, the lighting testimony could bear on a different alleged hazard, but the record does not identify any concealed defect other than the absence of the handrail, which Friese already knew about.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Remove any factual claim that the stairwell was undisputedly adequately lit. Reframe the argument so the lighting testimony, even if credited, does not matter because Friese knew the railing was absent and did not identify lighting as the cause of the fall.

A missing handrail may violate a local building code, and such a violation is negligence per se, providing an independent basis for liability that the brief fails to rebut.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If a statutory duty under (A)(1) exists, the brief's conclusion that no statutory duty applies is incomplete, and summary judgment cannot be granted on that ground.

attacks_proposed.argument: The cases cited by the brief—St. Germain v. Newell and Taylor v. Alexander—address only whether a missing handrail renders premises uninhabitable under R.C. 5321.04(A)(2). They do not address the duty under R.C. 5321.04(A)(1) to comply with building codes, nor do they foreclose a claim based on a code violation. The brief's reliance on them is therefore misplaced.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: The brief's statutory argument is overbroad and fails to defeat a potential negligence per se claim under (A)(1), leaving a viable theory of liability.

attacks_proposed.argument: Friese's personal injury claim is not a compulsory counterclaim under Civ.R. 13(A) because it does not arise from the same transaction or occurrence as Baker's municipal-court claims for eviction and monetary damages. The fall occurred months before the eviction action, and the landlord's claims for back rent and property damage are separate occurrences lacking the requisite logical relation. The brief's cited authority, including Sherman v. Pearson, is distinguishable because there the injury occurred in a common area and the claims were more intertwined.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If the claim was not compulsory, res judicata does not bar the current action, and the case may proceed.

attacks_proposed.argument: The Chardon Municipal Court likely lacked subject-matter jurisdiction over a personal injury tort claim exceeding its monetary limit, and such a claim is not a compulsory counterclaim if it could not have been brought in that court. Municipal courts have limited equity jurisdiction only in actions at law based on contract, and a tort claim for personal injury is not contract-based. Thus, the claim could not have been asserted in the prior action, and res judicata does not bar it.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If the municipal court lacked jurisdiction, the claim was not a compulsory counterclaim, and the current action is not precluded.

attacks_proposed.argument: The brief conflates Friese's actual knowledge of the missing handrail with the open-and-obvious doctrine. Even if he knew of the condition, that does not relieve Baker of her statutory duty to comply with building codes. The open-and-obvious doctrine is a common-law defense that does not apply to statutory negligence per se claims.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: The brief's central premise—that knowledge bars the claim—is legally insufficient to defeat a statutory duty claim, so summary judgment cannot be granted on that basis.

attacks_proposed.argument: The brief fails to develop the factual connection between Friese's injury claim and Baker's municipal-court claims. The record shows the injury occurred on January 16, 2021, while the eviction action was filed on May 25, 2021, and sought May rent and property damage. There is no evidence that the injury and the rent/property damage claims share a common nucleus of operative facts, making the logical-relation test unsatisfied.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: Without a sufficient factual link, the res judicata argument collapses, and the claim is not barred.

judge_assessments.assessment: The legal premise is correct: an established violation of R.C. 5321.04(A)(1) may constitute negligence per se, to which open and obvious is not a defense. The cited sources also identify an Ohio case applying a local-code handrail requirement to basement stairs. But the attack is conditional on matters not established here: Friese must have pleaded or otherwise preserved a statutory theory, identify an applicable code requiring a railing on this staircase, and produce evidence of a violation and causation. The brief expressly says the complaint alleges only invitee premises liability, and the supplied record identifies no governing code. If Friese supplies that foundation, Baker could lose the open-and-obvious ground; without it, Armstrong remains responsive to the claim actually pleaded.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The complaint relies on invitee premises liability, Friese knew the railing was absent, and Armstrong makes an observable or known hazard a no-duty condition. The brief also asserts that Friese pleaded no higher landlord duty.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Examine the complaint, any amendments, the applicable Thompson Township or state building code, the property's construction date and grandfathering provisions, and evidence that the staircase violated the governing code.

judge_assessments.assessment: This exposes a real overstatement in the brief. R.C. 5321.04(A)(2)'s habitability duty is not the statute's only potentially relevant duty; subsection (A)(1) separately requires compliance with applicable safety codes, and a qualifying violation can support negligence per se. Thus, proving that a missing handrail does not alone make premises uninhabitable does not establish that Ohio law never requires a handrail. Still, Friese cannot defeat summary judgment merely by saying a code may exist. On this record, no particular applicable code or violation is identified, and the brief contends no statutory claim was pleaded. Baker risks losing her categorical 'no statutory duty' proposition, but not necessarily the motion itself.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: R.C. 5321.04(A)(2) requires fit and habitable premises; St. Germain and Taylor hold that a missing handrail alone does not make premises substantially or wholly uninhabitable. The brief also says the complaint alleges only invitee premises liability.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Determine whether Friese pleaded an R.C. 5321.04(A)(1) theory and identify the specific building or safety code applicable to this staircase.

judge_assessments.assessment: A genuine lighting dispute could prevent a finding that the stair condition was objectively open and obvious, but the attack does not presently establish that dispute because the contrary deposition passage is not reproduced. More importantly, the pleaded hazard is the absence of a handrail, which Friese admittedly knew about and had reported to Baker. Poor lighting would not conceal the known absence of a railing. The attack becomes more consequential only if Friese identifies a different hazard—such as an obscured step configuration—as the cause of the fall. That is difficult on the quoted testimony, where he did not know why he missed the step. Baker risks losing the objective open-and-obvious characterization, but her actual-knowledge argument remains.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The staircase had a stairwell light and an outside window; Friese turned on the light, used the stairs three to four times daily for nearly four years, knew there was no railing, and could not say with certainty why he fell.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Review the complete deposition testimony concerning lighting, visibility of individual steps, the precise alleged hazard, and causation.

judge_assessments.assessment: The criticism is legally accurate but duplicates a3. St. Germain and Taylor support only the narrower proposition that a missing handrail, standing alone, does not violate the habitability duty in R.C. 5321.04(A)(2). They do not eliminate a separate claim based on an applicable code under subsection (A)(1). But the limitation in those cases does not itself establish that an applicable code existed, was violated, or was pleaded here. The brief loses its categorical statement that landlords have no statutory handrail duty, not necessarily summary judgment.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief relies on St. Germain and Taylor to conclude broadly that defective or missing handrails do not violate statutory landlord duties.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Same inquiry as a3: the pleadings and the specific code governing this property would determine whether the distinction affects the result.

judge_assessments.assessment: The stated rule is correct for a properly supported negligence-per-se claim: Friese's knowledge would not excuse Baker's violation of a statutory duty. But the attack duplicates a1 and assumes the missing premise—that Friese has a viable R.C. 5321.04(A)(1) claim based on an identified code violation. For the common-law invitee claim actually described in the brief, actual knowledge strongly supports Baker's no-duty position. Friese stands to gain little by pressing this point without first establishing the statutory claim.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: Because Friese knew the handrail was absent, recognized the potential danger, and repeatedly used the stairs, Baker owed no common-law duty to warn him of that condition.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Confirm whether a statutory negligence-per-se claim was pleaded and whether an applicable handrail code was violated.

judge_assessments.assessment: The cited source does not support the proposed distinction. It indicates that Civ.R. 13(A) generally does not apply when an eviction complaint seeks possession only, but Baker's prior action also sought and obtained monetary damages. More importantly, the brief cites Adams, involving a tenant's later personal-injury claim for a fall down steps, and Sherman, holding that a stair-fall claim was logically related to a landlord's prior eviction-and-rent action because both concerned rights and duties arising from the tenancy. The fact that Friese fell before the later action strengthens, rather than weakens, the compulsory-counterclaim argument because the claim already existed. The common-area distinction does not answer the stated reasoning of Sherman. This attack would likely fail unless the actual municipal complaint reveals materially different claims or procedural facts.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The prior action sought eviction and monetary damages arising from the tenancy, proceeded to judgment on the damages claim, and Adams and Sherman treat analogous tenant injury claims as compulsory counterclaims.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Review the complete opinions in Adams and Sherman and the precise factual allegations in Baker's municipal-court complaint.

judge_assessments.assessment: The brief's factual development is concise, but not absent: it identifies the preexisting injury, the same landlord-tenant relationship and premises, the later claims for rent and property damage, and a final damages judgment. It then cites factually close cases applying the logical-relation test to tenancy-based injury and rent claims. Merely observing that the fall and nonpayment occurred on different dates does not overcome those authorities. Friese would need to show that the governing appellate authority requires substantially overlapping evidence rather than the broader tenancy-based logical relation used in Sherman and Adams. On the presented authorities, this attack is unlikely to defeat preclusion.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: Friese's injury arose from his tenancy and leased premises; Baker's prior damages claims arose from the same tenancy; and analogous Ohio cases hold such personal-injury claims compulsory.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The full prior complaint, judgment, and trial record would show how closely Baker's rent and property-damage theories related to the condition of the premises.

judge_assessments.assessment: The cited source concerns a municipal court's limited equitable jurisdiction and does not show that the court lacked jurisdiction over a legal claim for personal-injury damages. Ohio municipal courts can hear tort claims within their monetary jurisdiction, and Ohio procedure provides a mechanism for handling a counterclaim exceeding that jurisdiction rather than simply making it noncompulsory. The record also does not establish the amount of Friese's claim at the time a responsive pleading was due. Thus, neither the cited authority nor the current facts support this jurisdictional escape from Civ.R. 13(A). Raising it without the governing monetary-jurisdiction and transfer rules would undermine the opposition's stronger arguments.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief treats Friese's injury claim as an available compulsory counterclaim in the municipal damages action but does not separately discuss the municipal court's monetary jurisdiction.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Confirm the municipal court's monetary limit, the amount of Friese's claim when the counterclaim should have been filed, and the operation of Civ.R. 13(J) or other transfer procedures.

judge_assessments.assessment: This reverses the burdens. Baker did not assume an affirmative obligation to prove every element of a statutory claim merely by addressing R.C. 5321.04 defensively. Friese would have to establish notice and a reasonable opportunity to repair if those are elements of his chosen statutory theory. In any event, the brief states that Friese allegedly told Baker before the injury that the staircase needed a railing, so it does not wholly omit notice; the unresolved issue would be timing and opportunity to repair. This is not a defect in Baker's motion unless Friese first produces evidence supporting the statutory claim and Baker fails to negate it under Civ.R. 56.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: Friese allegedly told Baker before his injury that the staircase needed a railing, but the brief does not specify when that notice occurred.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Confirm the elements and notice exceptions applicable to the particular subsection and code theory, then review the complaint and deposition for the timing of notice.

judge_assessments.assessment: A statutory 'consequence' such as rent abatement or a possession defense is not an element Baker had to plead in seeking summary judgment against a personal-injury complaint. Friese seeks personal-injury damages, and Ohio authority recognizes damages as potentially available when a proven R.C. 5321.04 violation proximately causes injury. The actual dispute is whether Friese pleaded and can prove a statutory violation, not whether Baker identified a separate statutory remedy. This attack would not be reached.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief acknowledges that Friese seeks personal-injury compensation but argues there was no actionable statutory handrail duty and that the claim is otherwise barred.

results.verdict: Mostly persuasive on the pleaded premises-liability theory,
results.assessment: The brief is solid on the claim as pleaded: it frames the case as ordinary invitee premises liability, leans on Armstrong, and has useful factual support from Friese’s long-term familiarity with the stairs and admitted knowledge that there was no handrail. Its main weakness is overclaiming that no statutory duty matters at all; the challenges show R.C. 5321.04(A)(1) and any applicable code violation are a real gap if Friese preserved that theory and can identify a specific code requiring a railing. The second weakness is factual: the lighting testimony could muddy the open-and-obvious analysis if Friese ties it to a concealed hazard, though the record as supplied still leaves Baker’s actual-knowledge argument intact.

challenges.opponent_argument: The open and obvious doctrine does not bar Friese's claim because Baker, as a landlord, had a statutory duty under R.C. 5321.04 to maintain the premises in a fit and habitable condition, which includes compliance with building codes requiring handrails on stairways. A violation of R.C. 5321.04 constitutes negligence per se and obviates the open-and-obvious doctrine. See Mann v. Northgate Investors, L.L.C., 138 Ohio St.3d 175, 2014-Ohio-89, ¶ 33; Robinson v. Bates, 112 Ohio St.3d 17, 2006-Ohio-6362. Thus, even if the absence of a handrail was open and obvious, Baker's failure to install one in violation of statutory duties precludes summary judgment on this ground.
challenges.why_it_matters: If the open and obvious doctrine is inapplicable due to a statutory violation, Baker cannot rely on it to defeat the premises-liability claim, and summary judgment must be denied.

challenges.judge_assessment: The legal principle is sound but the necessary predicate is absent on this record. Mann supports displacement of the open-and-obvious doctrine for negligence per se based on R.C. 5321.04(A)(3), and Robinson addresses statutory landlord duties. The retrieved material also shows that an applicable municipal code can impose a handrail duty. But the complaint passages and summary-judgment record identified here do not allege or establish any applicable building code, a code violation, or that this staircase was a common area governed by R.C. 5321.04(A)(3). The staircase appears to have served Friese's basement apartment, and the attack cannot simply assume a statutory violation. Without that proof, Armstrong remains available against the pleaded common-law theory. Baker's statement that she had no duty to install a handrail is potentially overbroad, but this attack does not presently create a triable statutory claim.
challenges.suggested_response: Friese has not pointed the Court to any admissible evidence in this record showing a violation of R.C. 5321.04 or any applicable building code provision requiring a handrail on these basement steps. His complaint sounds in common-law premises liability, and on that theory Armstrong controls: a landowner owes no duty to warn of a condition that is known to the invitee or so open and obvious that the invitee may reasonably be expected to discover it. Here, Friese’s own testimony shows that he knew the stairway, used it repeatedly, and was aware of its condition before the fall. Absent proof of a statutory or code violation, the open-and-obvious doctrine remains a complete defense to the pleaded claim.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Narrow this argument to the common-law open-and-obvious rule and do not invoke R.C. 5321.04 unless the record is supplemented with an actual code or statutory violation. On the present record, the safer point is that Friese pleaded no statutory theory and the excerpts filed do not show any applicable handrail code provision or common-area duty that would displace Armstrong.

challenges.opponent_argument: The record does not establish that the absence of a handrail was an open and obvious hazard. The deposition testimony only shows that Friese was subjectively aware of the staircase's condition and had told Baker it needed a railing. The open and obvious doctrine requires an objective assessment of whether the hazard itself would be discoverable by a reasonable person. The record lacks evidence, such as expert testimony or photographs, demonstrating that the lack of a handrail was observable and apparent as a danger. Without such evidence, Baker cannot meet her burden on summary judgment.
challenges.why_it_matters: If the hazard was not open and obvious as a matter of law, Baker owed a duty to warn or protect, and summary judgment is improper.

challenges.judge_assessment: This attack does not overcome the undisputed evidence of actual knowledge. Ohio's rule covers dangers known to the invitee as well as dangers objectively open and obvious. Friese allegedly used the stairs three to four times daily for nearly four years, knew there was no handrail, and claimed that he had told Baker the staircase needed one. That evidence goes beyond mere familiarity with a staircase and indicates recognition of the asserted danger. Photographs or expert testimony are not categorically required to establish an obvious missing handrail, and the lack of such evidence is not material where the plaintiff admits both awareness of the condition and concern about it. The attack might matter if the relevant hazard were some different, concealed defect, but the pleaded hazard identified here is the missing handrail.
challenges.suggested_response: The summary-judgment record establishes Friese’s actual knowledge of the stairway condition. He testified that he used the stairs three to four times each day, lived in the basement apartment for nearly four years, and was ‘well aware of the condition of the basement stairwell’ before his fall. He also testified that, when he returned from the store, he turned on the light, turned around to close the door, and then missed the step. That testimony defeats any claim that the alleged hazard was unknown to him. The open-and-obvious doctrine does not turn on whether Baker submitted photographs or expert testimony where the plaintiff admits repeated familiarity with the condition he now claims was dangerous.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Delete the unsupported assertion that Friese told Baker the staircase needed a railing unless you can cite record support for it. Keep the argument anchored in his deposition admissions that he used the stairs repeatedly and knew their condition before the fall.

challenges.opponent_argument: The record does not demonstrate that Friese's personal injury claim and Baker's claims for back rent and property damage arose from the same transaction or occurrence. The injury occurred on January 16, 2021, from a fall on the stairs, while Baker's municipal court action sought eviction and monetary damages for non-payment of rent and property damage. The brief merely asserts a logical relation based on the tenancy, but the record contains no evidence linking the specific incident to the financial disputes. Without such a connection, the claims are not part of the same transaction or occurrence, and the personal injury claim was not a compulsory counterclaim.
challenges.why_it_matters: If the claims are not logically related, res judicata does not bar the later suit, and summary judgment must be denied.

record_sources.title: record-01-record
record_sources.quote: "On May 25, 2021, Baker filed an eviction action, which also included a claim for both back rent and for damage to the premises." ... "The second cause of action proceeded to trial on July 21, 2021, at which Friese did not appear. The trial court took evidence and granted judgment in favor of Baker for the sum of $5,336.00 together with statutory interest and court costs."

challenges.judge_assessment: The cited Ohio cases substantially answer this objection. Adams and Sherman, as described in the brief, involved later personal-injury claims arising from stairway falls and earlier landlord actions seeking eviction plus monetary relief; both treated the injury claims as compulsory counterclaims because the parties' rights and duties were logically related through the tenancy. Baker's prior action likewise included monetary claims, not possession alone. The attack's demand for a direct factual connection between the fall and the unpaid-rent or property-damage events is narrower than the logical-relation test applied in those authorities. Although the brief's application is concise, it identifies the same tenancy, premises, parties, preexisting injury, and subsequent damages action. On the presented authorities, merely emphasizing that the events occurred on different dates would not defeat preclusion.
challenges.suggested_response: The relevant question is not whether Baker’s municipal-court action and Friese’s injury claim were identical in label, but whether they arose out of the same rental relationship and the same premises. The record shows that Friese’s alleged injury occurred while he was renting Baker’s basement apartment, and that Baker later filed an action in the Chardon Municipal Court seeking both eviction and monetary damages arising from that tenancy. Because Baker’s suit was not limited to possession, Civ.R. 13(A) was implicated, and Friese was required to assert any logically related claim arising from the tenancy in that action. The resulting judgment on Baker’s damages claim is now final, and Friese may not bring a later suit based on the same rental relationship and premises.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Keep the res judicata point, but tie it more tightly to what the record actually shows: the same tenancy, the same premises, and Baker’s prior action for eviction and monetary damages. If you want to preserve the compulsory-counterclaim theory, the brief should rely on the authorities already cited and on the treatise statement that Civ.R. 13(A) applies where the landlord’s action includes monetary damages, not possession alone.

attacks_proposed.argument: The open and obvious doctrine does not bar Friese's claim because Baker, as a landlord, had a statutory duty under R.C. 5321.04 to maintain the premises in a fit and habitable condition, which includes compliance with building codes requiring handrails on stairways. A violation of R.C. 5321.04 constitutes negligence per se and obviates the open-and-obvious doctrine. See Mann v. Northgate Investors, L.L.C., 138 Ohio St.3d 175, 2014-Ohio-89, ¶ 33; Robinson v. Bates, 112 Ohio St.3d 17, 2006-Ohio-6362. Thus, even if the absence of a handrail was open and obvious, Baker's failure to install one in violation of statutory duties precludes summary judgment on this ground.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If the open and obvious doctrine is inapplicable due to a statutory violation, Baker cannot rely on it to defeat the premises-liability claim, and summary judgment must be denied.

attacks_proposed.argument: The brief fails to establish that the Chardon Municipal Court had subject-matter jurisdiction over Friese's personal injury claim. Municipal courts have limited jurisdiction, and the brief does not show that the amount in controversy fell within the municipal court's monetary limit or that the claim was otherwise within its jurisdiction. If the municipal court lacked jurisdiction over the personal injury claim, it could not have been a compulsory counterclaim, and res judicata does not apply.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: Without jurisdiction, the prior court could not have adjudicated the claim, so the failure to assert it there does not bar the current action.

judge_assessments.coverageNote: The municipal-court complaint and the full opinions in Adams and Sherman would confirm whether any material distinction exists concerning the nature of Baker's monetary claims or the scope of the tenancy relationship.

judge_assessments.assessment: The cited source does not establish a jurisdictional defect; it says municipal courts have limited jurisdiction but that their jurisdiction encompasses virtually all landlord-tenant claims. The attack identifies neither the damages Friese sought nor any other fact showing that the municipal court could not entertain the counterclaim. Moreover, Ohio municipal-court procedure generally provides a mechanism for handling a counterclaim exceeding the court's monetary jurisdiction, so an unspecified possibility that the injury claim exceeded the limit does not establish that it was noncompulsory. Baker produced a municipal-court judgment on the landlord's monetary claim, and Friese's nonappearance does not itself undermine finality. A concrete jurisdictional barrier could defeat preclusion, but none is shown here.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief establishes that the municipal action included a monetary-damages claim, proceeded to trial, and resulted in a final judgment. It does not separately discuss the municipal court's monetary limit or the procedure for an oversized counterclaim.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: The prayer for relief in Friese's current complaint, the Chardon Municipal Court's statutory monetary jurisdiction in 2021, and Civ.R. 13(J) transfer practice would conclusively resolve the point.

judge_assessments.assessment: This is only a conclusion dependent on attacks a1 through a4 and identifies no independent factual dispute or legal defect under Civ.R. 56. Because the proposed challenges do not defeat either defense on the presented record, this derivative assertion adds nothing. If one substantive defense fails, the court still must consider whether the other independently supports judgment.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The motion requests summary judgment under Civ.R. 56 based on two asserted complete defenses: open and obvious or known danger, and claim preclusion through failure to assert a compulsory counterclaim.

results.verdict: persuasive on the common-law defenses, but exposed on the st
results.assessment: As written, the brief is strongest where it leans on Friese’s actual knowledge of the stairway and on the preclusion theory tied to the prior landlord action; those points track the cited authorities and the record described in the challenges. Its main weakness is the attempt to defeat the open-and-obvious defense by invoking R.C. 5321.04 and a handrail-code violation without record support for any applicable code, violation, or common-area duty. It is also somewhat overconfident on res judicata, because the challenge says the necessary logical-relation analysis is doing the work, not a direct factual identity between the fall and the rent dispute. The research did not settle any additional factual predicate for the statutory claim.
